blocks.content: Explore a finished dashboard on Grafana Play, panel by panel, to see what it monitors and how each panel serves that purpose.
Explore a finished dashboard, panel by panel, to see what it monitors and how each panel serves that purpose.
Open **Grafana Dashboard**.
Find the **Memory / CPU** panel, top left.
This panel answers the question: How much memory and CPU is the server using, and how has that changed over time?
Focus on the **Memory** gauge in the bottom row.
This panel answers the question: How close is memory use to its limit? It's the same resource as the first panel, shown as one value within a range instead of a line over time.
Focus on the **logins** panel.
Notice the **server requests** panel.

These two panels answer the question: How many people are signing in, and how many requests is the server handling, over time? They measure what the service is doing rather than the machine it runs on.
Focus on the **Google hits**, top right.

Four panels carry this title: two bar gauges on the right, and a gauge and a third bar gauge in the bottom row. One title, four displays. Notice that nothing on the panels says how they differ, so the viewer can't tell which one to read.

The titles are what the viewer has to go on. Read together, they describe one server: the resources it uses and the traffic it handles. That is what this dashboard monitors, and it's the question to hold in mind as you read each panel.
You've seen what this dashboard monitors, how each panel's title tells you what it measures, and which panels repeat. Next, see how a panel gets the data behind its title.
Explore a panel to find the query inside it, the data source it runs against, and the format its result comes back in.

blocks.title: Find the query and its data source

blocks.content: Open **Base Query (A) - Total CPU Usage** on the **SQL Expressions Showcase** dashboard.
Open the panel menu and select **Edit**.
Notice the data source for query **A**. It's a Prometheus data source, so Grafana sends this query to Prometheus.

Read the query: `sum(rate(process_cpu_seconds_total[5m]))`. It selects one metric, `process_cpu_seconds_total`, turns it into a per-second rate, and sums the result across every instance. The data source holds far more data than this. The query reduces it to the one series the panel needs.

Below the query, find the query options and read **Format**. For this panel it's **Time series**, the shape the result comes back in. The visualization decides how that shape is drawn, so the same time series result could feed a graph, a stat, or a gauge.
Return to the panel.
You've found a panel's query, the data source it runs against, and its result format. The query chooses the data. The visualization only presents it.
Explore the Memory gauge to find its unit setting and connect it to the suffix on its value.

blocks.title: Connect the setting to the label

blocks.content: Open the **Memory** gauge and notice the B suffix beside its value.
Open the **Memory** panel menu and select **Edit**. Expand **Standard options** if it's collapsed.
Find **Unit** and read its **bytes(IEC)** setting.

The **Memory** panel formats its numeric value as bytes. B means bytes; larger values can use units such as KiB or MiB. Unit formatting changes the display, not the query's data, and doesn't change timestamps into byte values.

Changing bytes to percent wouldn't calculate memory utilization. It would mislabel the existing values. The unit must match what the query measures; a utilization query would need to return a proportion of capacity.
Return to the **Memory** gauge.
You've located Unit and distinguished the displayed label from the unchanged data. Match the unit to what the query measures before interpreting a value.
Explore a dashboard to see which of its panels measure the machine's resources, the USE method, and which measure the service as its users experience it, the RED method.
Open **Sample Website Dashboard**.
Find the **Memory / CPU** panel.
Focus on the **Memory** gauge.
Both measure a machine's resources, so they belong to the USE method. Both show how much of the resource is in use: utilization.
Focus on the **server requests** panel.
Focus on the **client side full page load** panel.
Both measure the service as its users experience it, so they belong to the RED method. Requests over time is the rate. Page load time is the duration.
RED has a third measurement, errors. No panel counts failing requests, so this dashboard can't tell you whether requests are failing.
The four golden signals name the same three service measurements as RED, as traffic, errors, and latency, and add saturation: how close a resource is to its capacity. No panel here shows that either.

The remaining panels, **logins**, **Google hits**, **Support calls**, and **Sign ups**, are business measurements. Neither method covers them. The methods tell you what a health dashboard needs, not what every dashboard must contain.
You've seen which panels measure resources, which measure the service, and what a health dashboard would still need. The question a dashboard answers tells you which method it needs.
